title: Special Issues — Intercompany Eliminations, FX & Fair Value (CMA P2-A · feeds FAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — two real balances that must vanish on consolidation

Real MBG facts: the intercompany payable on MBG account 89010 is reciprocal with Riverton's intercompany receivable 89011, and MBG's note receivable 89012 is reciprocal with Riverton's note payable 89013. Both reciprocal pairs tie at their checkpoints — MBG 89010 and Riverton 89011 each at $850,000.00, and MBG 89012 and Riverton 89013 each at $12,000.00 — equal and opposite, so they eliminate on consolidation. (A later run found a real $400.00 drift on the note pair, a live example of the very control this week is about.) That is not an accident — it is the control that lets the balances be eliminated in any consolidated view. This week covers the analysis issues that sit outside the standard ratios: intercompany eliminations, foreign currency, and fair value.

Intercompany eliminations

When related entities transact, each side records its half: MBG owes Riverton, so MBG carries a payable (89010) and Riverton carries the matching receivable (89011). If you simply added the two entities together, consolidated assets and liabilities would both be overstated by the same intercompany amount — a company cannot owe or be owed by itself. Consolidation therefore eliminates reciprocal intercompany receivables and payables, notes, and any intercompany revenue/expense or unrealized profit.

The control discipline: the reciprocal accounts must be equal and opposite before elimination. MBG 89010 must equal Riverton 89011; MBG note receivable 89012 must equal Riverton note payable 89013. A non-zero net would flag a missing entry, a timing cutoff, or a posting error — you investigate the difference rather than plug it. The ICP pair nets to zero, but the note pair's $400.00 drift is exactly such a flag: it must be investigated, not plugged. Note that this is distinct from performance comparison (week 3), where the entities stay separate; elimination applies only to the consolidated view.

This is also a useful sense of off-balance-sheet: the intercompany note that is a real asset on MBG's own books does not appear at all on the consolidated balance sheet because it nets against Riverton's payable.

Foreign currency (ASC 830)

The functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which an entity operates; the reporting currency is the one the financial statements are presented in. Three situations the exam separates:

  • Foreign-currency transaction — MBG buys equipment priced in euros and settles later. The exchange-rate change between purchase and settlement creates a transaction gain or loss recognized in net income.
  • Translation — a foreign subsidiary keeps books in its functional currency and is translated to the reporting currency using the current-rate method. The resulting translation adjustment goes to other comprehensive income (the cumulative translation adjustment), not net income.
  • Remeasurement — books kept in a currency other than the functional currency are remeasured into the functional currency, and those gains/losses do hit net income.

The exam trap is the destination: transaction and remeasurement effects flow through income; translation under the current-rate method parks in OCI as CTA until the foreign operation is sold.

Fair value (ASC 820)

Fair value is an exit price in an orderly transaction between market participants. The measurement hierarchy ranks the inputs, not the assets:

  • Level 1 — quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities (most reliable).
  • Level 2 — observable inputs other than Level 1: quoted prices for similar items, quoted prices in inactive markets, or other observable data.
  • Level 3 — unobservable inputs, such as management's own discounted-cash-flow assumptions (least reliable, most disclosure).

A contractor estimating the fair value of a custom, non-traded asset by its own cash-flow model is using Level 3 inputs and must disclose the assumptions and sensitivity.

Off-balance-sheet items and disclosure

Historically, operating leases, certain guarantees, and special-purpose entities kept obligations off the balance sheet. Under ASC 842, a lessee now recognizes a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for operating leases, bringing most lease obligations on-balance-sheet. Items that remain off the face of the statements but affect risk — performance and payment bonds, surety commitments, retainage obligations, and contract backlog — are addressed through disclosure. An analyst adjusts leverage and coverage for material off-balance-sheet commitments before concluding on solvency.

A worked foreign-currency transaction

Walk the mechanics that the destination rule sits on top of. Suppose MBG orders specialized equipment from a European supplier for €100,000 when the spot rate is €1 = $1.08. At the order/recognition date it records the asset and payable at $108,000 (€100,000 × 1.08). Sixty days later, at settlement, the rate has moved to €1 = $1.12, so MBG must pay $112,000 to buy the euros. The $4,000 difference is a foreign-currency transaction loss recognized in net income — the dollar weakened against the euro, so settling the same €100,000 obligation cost more dollars, and the loss is real cash. Had the rate fallen to $1.05, MBG would record a $3,000 transaction gain. The asset's recorded cost stays $108,000 either way; only the settlement of the monetary liability produces the income-statement effect. This is the income-versus-OCI line drawn precisely: a settled transaction hits earnings, while translating a foreign subsidiary under the current-rate method would instead park the adjustment in OCI.

Fair-value disclosure and analyst adjustments

Beyond classifying inputs as Level 1, 2, or 3, FAR-style reporting requires disclosure proportional to subjectivity: Level 3 measurements demand the valuation technique, the significant unobservable inputs, and often a sensitivity analysis showing how the estimate moves with the assumptions. The less observable the input, the more an informed reader should discount management's number — a recurring theme from the CMA data-integrity scars.

For off-balance-sheet items, a careful analyst re-leverages the statements before judging solvency: capitalize the present value of material operating commitments and guarantees, add them to debt, and recompute debt-to-equity and times-interest-earned on the adjusted figures. A contractor that looks comfortably leveraged on its face statements can look very different once surety obligations, large purchase commitments, and guarantees are pulled into view. Reading the face of the statements is necessary; reading the notes is where the real exposure — and the real exam points — live.

Where each effect lands — a quick map

Because the destination is the most-tested point, hold this map for the items in this lesson: a settled foreign-currency transaction and a remeasurement into the functional currency both hit net income; a current-rate translation of a foreign operation goes to OCI as the cumulative translation adjustment. Fair value is ranked by input observability — Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable — with required disclosure rising as observability falls. Intercompany receivables, payables, and notes eliminate entirely on consolidation, so they never inflate the consolidated balance sheet. And under ASC 842, the operating lease that once sat off-balance-sheet now appears on it as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Fix these destinations in memory and most FAR foreign-currency, fair-value, and lease questions resolve on sight; the arithmetic is usually the easy part.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR tests these cold: eliminate intercompany balances and unrealized profit in consolidation, place a foreign-currency effect in income versus OCI, and classify a fair-value input as Level 1, 2, or 3. The reciprocal-account control here (89010↔89011, 89012↔89013 must be equal before elimination) is the same logic FAR uses for consolidation worksheets, and ASC 830/820/842 are core FAR standards.

Practice and recap

  1. Eliminate reciprocal intercompany receivables/payables and notes in the consolidated view; verify they are equal before elimination.
  2. Route a foreign-currency transaction or remeasurement gain to income; route a current-rate translation adjustment to OCI (CTA).
  3. Classify a fair-value input as Level 1, 2, or 3 by its observability.
  4. Recognize operating leases on-balance-sheet under ASC 842 and adjust for remaining off-balance-sheet commitments.

Recap: MBG's reciprocal intercompany pairs are equal and opposite (89010/89011 at $850,000.00; 89012/89013 at $12,000.00) so they eliminate cleanly on consolidation — and the note pair's $400.00 drift shows the control catching a real difference. Foreign-currency effects split between income and OCI by type, fair value is ranked by input observability, and most lease obligations now sit on the balance sheet.

quiz.title: Intercompany Eliminations, FX, and Fair Value

questions.q: MBG's intercompany payable (89010) is reciprocal with Riverton's receivable (89011). On consolidation these balances are:
questions.explain: Reciprocal intercompany balances are eliminated so consolidated assets and liabilities are not overstated.

questions.q: Why must MBG 89010 equal Riverton 89011 before elimination?
choices: Because a non-zero net flags a missing entry, timing, or posting error
questions.explain: Reciprocal accounts must be equal and opposite; a difference signals an error to investigate, not plug.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary's statements are translated using the current-rate method. The translation adjustment is reported in:
questions.explain: Current-rate translation adjustments go to OCI as the cumulative translation adjustment, not income.

questions.q: MBG buys equipment denominated in euros and settles 60 days later at a different rate. The exchange difference is:
choices: A transaction gain or loss in net income
Added to the asset cost permanently
questions.explain: A settled foreign-currency transaction produces a transaction gain/loss recognized in net income.

questions.q: A quoted price in an active market for an identical asset is which fair-value level?
questions.explain: Level 1 inputs are quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

questions.q: Management values a custom, non-traded asset using its own discounted-cash-flow assumptions. These are:
questions.explain: Unobservable, entity-developed inputs such as a private DCF are Level 3 and require expanded disclosure.

questions.q: Under ASC 842, a lessee accounts for an operating lease by:
choices: Keeping it entirely off the balance sheet
Recognizing a right-of-use asset and a lease liability
questions.explain: ASC 842 brings operating leases on-balance-sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.
